source: Stops chosen by CAIRN on the HiRISE terrain and imagery (no rover has visited Deuteronilus Mensae)

rover.name: Pressurised rover
rover.description: EVA start, end and radiation shelter. Parked on the flat plain north of the debris apron, 500 m east of a fresh 700 m crater.
rover.science: From the plain the crew sees the toe of the apron to the south: the edge of a glacier buried under rock debris, rising away from the landing area.
rover.whyHumans: Landing on the flat plain and driving to the edge of the ice keeps the heavy lander off the rough apron and away from the crater.

toe.name: Apron edge · glacier toe
toe.description: Where the lobate debris apron ends on the plain. To the south the ground starts to rise and the surface turns into a maze of ridges.
toe.science: Radar on NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (SHARAD) showed that lobate debris aprons in this region are glaciers: water ice under a cover of rock debris (Plaut et al. 2009). At the toe the apron is thinnest and meets the ground the crew landed on.
toe.whyHumans: A crew can dig through the debris cover and measure how deep the ice starts: the number that decides whether a base can mine it for water.

brain.name: Brain terrain on the apron
brain.description: A maze of ridges and troughs, metres across, covering the apron. It is named for its likeness to brain coral.
brain.science: Brain terrain forms on ice-rich ground. One explanation is that ice under the debris sublimates unevenly, so the surface sags into cells. Where the cells are open or closed may show where the ice lies closest to the surface.
brain.whyHumans: A geologist can trench one ridge and one trough in an hour — the quickest test of whether ice lies under a thin layer of rubble.

ring.name: Small ring crater
ring.description: A small rounded crater, about 60 m across, with a raised centre and a ring-shaped trough, among the brain terrain.
ring.science: Craters on ice-rich aprons often take this ring shape ('ring-mold craters'), thought to form when an impact strikes ice just below the debris (Kress & Head 2008). If this is one, the ice was shallow here when it formed.
ring.whyHumans: A short walk across the ring with ground-penetrating radar would test the idea on the spot.

rim.name: Crater rim · natural trench
rim.description: The south-east rim of a 700 m crater in the plain.
rim.science: The impact dug through the top tens of metres of the plain and threw that material onto the rim: a free sample of what lies under the landing site.
rim.whyHumans: From the rim a crew can sample deep material without drilling and look across the crater wall for layers.
